subject: chemistry

items.q: An atom of element X has the electron configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴. Which ion does X form in its ionic compounds?
items.correct: X²⁻
items.misconception: X²⁺
items.why: In everyday language 'gain' goes with 'plus' and 'loss' with 'minus', so students attach the sign of the charge to the direction of the change instead of to the charge of the electron. Confusion over the sign of ionic charge is widely reported in chemistry-education research. Count charges. The charge on an ion is (number of protons − number of electrons). A sulfur atom has 16 protons; after gaining two electrons it has 18 electrons, so its charge is 16 − 18 = −2 and it is S²⁻.
items.specStatementText: When metal atoms lose electrons, they form positive ions called cations. When non-metal atoms gain electrons, they form negative ions called anions.

items.q: Copper (atomic number 29) forms both Cu⁺ and Cu²⁺ ions. Which describes how a copper atom forms a Cu²⁺ ion?
items.correct: It loses its one 4s electron and one 3d electron.
items.misconception: It loses the two electrons from its 4s sublevel.
items.why: Students apply the Aufbau order mechanically and do not recall that chromium and copper are exceptions. Writing copper as [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s² is a frequently reported error. Copper is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. It forms Cu⁺ by losing its single 4s electron, giving [Ar] 3d¹⁰, and Cu²⁺ by losing that 4s electron and one 3d electron, giving [Ar] 3d⁹.
items.specStatementText: When metal atoms lose electrons, they form positive ions called cations. When non-metal atoms gain electrons, they form negative ions called anions.
items.random_wrong: It loses two 3d electrons and keeps its 4s one.

items.q: An iron atom has the electron configuration [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². Iron forms a sulfate with the formula Fe₂(SO₄)₃. What is the electron configuration of the iron ion in this compound? (4s⁰ shows that the 4s sublevel is empty.)
items.correct: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s⁰
items.misconception: [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s⁰
items.why: The 'swap and drop' (criss-cross) shortcut moves each ion's charge onto the OTHER ion as a subscript. Students who remember only that charges become subscripts attach each charge to its own ion. Confusion between charges and subscripts is widely reported. Subscripts count ions; they are chosen so that the charges cancel. To read a charge from a formula, use the known charge of the other ion: in Fe₂(SO₄)₃ the three sulfate ions carry 3 × (−2) = −6, so each of the two iron ions is +3.
items.specStatementText: When metal atoms lose electrons, they form positive ions called cations. When non-metal atoms gain electrons, they form negative ions called anions.

items.q: Which describes the ionic bonding in solid sodium chloride?
items.correct: Attraction between oppositely charged ions in all directions
items.misconception: Transfer of one electron from each sodium atom to a chlorine atom
items.why: Ionic bonding is usually introduced with 'dot-and-cross' diagrams showing an electron moving from sodium to chlorine, so students identify the bond with the transfer event. This is widely reported in chemistry-education research on ionic bonding. Separate the two ideas. Electron transfer (or any other route) produces ions; the bond is the attraction between the ions that results. The same NaCl lattice forms when a solution of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, made from quite different starting materials, is evaporated, and its bonds are identical.
items.specStatementText: The ionic bond is formed by electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.
items.random_wrong: Attraction joining each Na⁺ to one Cl⁻ in an NaCl molecule

items.q: A sample of sodium chloride is made by burning sodium in chlorine. In the solid, each Na⁺ ion has six Cl⁻ ions as its nearest neighbours, all at the same distance. Which statement about the bonding of one Na⁺ ion is correct?
items.correct: It is bonded to all six Cl⁻ ions, attracting each of them equally.
items.misconception: It is bonded only to the Cl⁻ ion that accepted its electron.
items.why: This combines the 'history' and 'just forces' conjectures in Taber's research on the molecular framework students use for ionic bonding: because bonding is taught through the transfer between one sodium atom and one chlorine atom, students treat that pair as bonded and the other neighbours as merely attracted. Ions carry no memory of where their electrons came from. The electrostatic attraction between a Na⁺ ion and a Cl⁻ ion depends only on their charges and the distance between them, and all six Cl⁻ neighbours are at the same distance, so all six attractions are the same.
items.specStatementText: The ionic bond is formed by electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.
items.random_wrong: It forms one bond, as its atom had one electron to give.

items.q: What is the formula of sodium phosphate, with a correct reason?
items.correct: Na₃PO₄, as three Na⁺ ions balance one PO₄³⁻ ion
items.misconception: Na₂PO₄, as phosphate has a 2− charge, like sulfate
items.why: Sulfate and carbonate are the -ate ions students meet most often, so they generalise their 2− charge to every ion with the same ending. Wrong charges on polyatomic ions are a common error in writing formulas. Learn each ion as a formula with its charge: NO₃⁻, HCO₃⁻, CO₃²⁻, SO₄²⁻, PO₄³⁻. For the -ate ions in this list the ending shows that the ion contains oxygen; it does not fix the charge.
items.specStatementText: The ionic bond is formed by electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.
items.random_wrong: NaPO₄, as one sodium ion pairs with one phosphate ion

items.q: Which formula is paired with its correct name?
items.correct: CuO, copper(II) oxide
items.misconception: Fe₂O₃, iron trioxide
items.why: Students learn prefix names for molecular compounds (carbon monoxide, sulfur trioxide) and apply the same rule to every compound. Using prefixes for ionic compounds is a common naming error. For an ionic compound name the ions, not the number of atoms: the cation name (with a Roman numeral for its charge if the metal forms more than one ion) followed by the anion name. The ratio is then fixed by the charges.
items.specStatementText: The ionic bond is formed by electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.

items.q: Which is the correct formula, including its charge, of a polyatomic ion in aqueous solution?
items.correct: OH⁻(aq)
items.misconception: NH₄⁻(aq)
items.why: Six of the seven polyatomic ions students learn are anions, and polyatomic ions are usually introduced as the 'second half' of a salt's name after the metal, so students generalise that every polyatomic ion is negative. Ammonium is NH₄⁺, formed when ammonia, NH₃, accepts an H⁺. In formulas and names it comes first, like a metal cation: (NH₄)₂SO₄ ammonium sulfate, NH₄NO₃ ammonium nitrate.
items.specStatementText: The ionic bond is formed by electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.

items.q: Aluminium, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p¹, reacts with oxygen, 1s² 2s² 2p⁴, to form aluminium oxide. Which gives its formula with a correct reason?
items.correct: Al₂O₃, as two Al³⁺ ions cancel the charge of three O²⁻
items.misconception: AlO, as each aluminium ion is paired with one oxide ion
items.why: The first ionic compounds students meet (NaCl, MgO, KBr) are 1 : 1, and ionic bonding is drawn with one cation beside one anion, so students do not balance charges when writing formulas. Always check that the charges sum to zero. Mg²⁺ with OH⁻: one Mg²⁺ (+2) needs two OH⁻ (2 × −1), so the formula is Mg(OH)₂.
items.specStatementText: The ionic bond is formed by electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.
items.random_wrong: Al₃O₂, as each ion's charge is written as its own subscript

items.q: The formula of magnesium chloride is MgCl₂. What does this formula represent?
items.correct: The 1 : 2 ratio of Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in a lattice
items.misconception: One molecule of one Mg atom bonded to two Cl atoms
items.why: Formulas are first met for molecular substances (H₂O, CO₂), and ionic bonding is taught with a single sodium–chlorine pair, so students read NaCl as a molecule. Belief in NaCl 'molecules' is widely reported in chemistry-education research, including Taber's work on the molecular framework. Students who picture molecules also often think that a substance boils or melts when the bonds within its molecules break, which is widely reported in chemistry-education research. An ionic formula is an empirical formula. In the lattice no Na⁺ ion belongs to any one Cl⁻ ion; each is surrounded by six ions of the opposite charge, and the pattern repeats throughout the crystal.
items.specStatementText: Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattice structures, represented by empirical formulas.
items.random_wrong: Mg²⁺ ions combined 1 : 1 with chlorine molecules, Cl₂

items.q: Which statement about the electrical conductivity of sodium chloride is correct?
items.correct: When molten, it conducts because its ions are free to move.
items.misconception: When molten, it conducts because it releases free electrons.
items.why: Electric current in wires is taught as a flow of electrons, so students assume every current is carried by electrons. The belief that electrons flow through electrolytes is widely reported in chemistry-education research on electrolysis. Electrons flow in the external circuit. Inside the molten or aqueous ionic compound there are no free electrons; the charge is carried by the movement of cations and anions to the electrodes.
items.specStatementText: Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattice structures, represented by empirical formulas.
items.random_wrong: When solid, it conducts because it is made up of charged ions.

items.q: Sodium chloride dissolves in water but not in hexane, C₆H₁₄. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: Polar water molecules are attracted to the ions and separate them from the lattice.
items.misconception: Water lowers the melting point of NaCl so that it melts at room temperature.
items.why: In everyday language sugar 'melts' in tea, and both processes turn a solid into something that flows, so students treat dissolving as melting. The confusion of dissolving with melting is widely reported in research on students' ideas about solutions. Melting involves one substance changing state when heated. Dissolving involves two substances: the ions become surrounded by solvent molecules. NaCl dissolves in water at room temperature because of the attraction between the ions and the polar water molecules.
items.specStatementText: Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattice structures, represented by empirical formulas.
items.random_wrong: The ions fit into the spaces between water molecules but not hexane ones.

items.q: Ionic radii (pm): Na⁺ 102, Cs⁺ 167, Ca²⁺ 100, Ba²⁺ 135, F⁻ 133, O²⁻ 140, S²⁻ 184. Which compound has the largest lattice enthalpy?
items.correct: CaO
items.misconception: NaF
items.why: Students who have practised radius comparisons for series such as NaF, NaCl and KCl, in which the charges are all the same, apply the size rule alone to compounds with different charges. Consider charge first, then radius. Doubling both charges roughly quadruples the attraction between the ions, which outweighs a difference of a few picometres in the ionic radii.
items.specStatementText: Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattice structures, represented by empirical formulas.

items.q: Lattice enthalpy is a measure of the strength of the ionic bonding in a compound. Ionic radii (pm): Na⁺ 102, K⁺ 138, F⁻ 133, Cl⁻ 181. Which shows the lattice enthalpies of NaF, NaCl and KCl in decreasing order?
items.correct: NaF > NaCl > KCl
items.misconception: KCl > NaCl > NaF
items.why: Students learn that London (dispersion) forces increase with the size of the molecules and that boiling points often rise with molar mass, and they carry 'bigger means stronger' over to ionic bonding. Electrostatic attraction between two ions increases with their charges and decreases as the distance between their centres increases. Larger ions sit further apart, so they attract each other less strongly.
items.specStatementText: Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattice structures, represented by empirical formulas.

items.q: Sodium chloride has a very low volatility: it does not evaporate at room temperature and melts only at 801 °C. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: Every ion is strongly attracted to many ions of opposite charge.
items.misconception: Its particles are so heavy that they cannot move fast enough to escape.
items.why: Boiling points often rise with molar mass within a series of similar molecular substances, and students take mass itself to be the cause of low volatility. Volatility depends on how strongly the particles are held together. In an ionic lattice each ion is strongly attracted to many oppositely charged ions, and overcoming these attractions needs much energy.
items.specStatementText: Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattice structures, represented by empirical formulas.
items.random_wrong: Evaporating it would break the strong bond in every NaCl molecule.

items.q: Which statement about the formula of an ionic compound is correct?
items.correct: Ammonium carbonate has the chemical formula (NH₄)₂CO₃
items.misconception: Ammonium hydrogencarbonate has the chemical formula (NH₄)₂HCO₃
items.why: Students treat the H in HCO₃ as a neutral atom that simply joins the ion, rather than as H⁺, so they keep the carbonate charge. Hydrogencarbonate is HCO₃⁻: CO₃²⁻ + H⁺ → HCO₃⁻. Its compounds show the 1− charge, for example sodium hydrogencarbonate NaHCO₃, compared with sodium carbonate Na₂CO₃.
items.specStatementText: The ionic bond is formed by electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.
items.random_wrong: Aluminium phosphate has the chemical formula Al₂(PO₄)₃

items.q: Could a sulfur atom, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴, form an S⁶⁺ ion in an ionic compound, since S⁶⁺ would have a full outer shell?
items.correct: No. In ionic compounds sulfur forms S²⁻ by gaining two electrons. Removing six electrons from a sulfur atom would require a very large amount of energy, and a full outer shell does not by itself make a species stable.
items.misconception: Atoms form ions by losing their outer-shell electrons to leave a full shell, as sodium does (Na → Na⁺), and any ion with a full outer shell is stable; so a sulfur atom can lose its six outer electrons to form S⁶⁺.
items.why: Students learn ion formation as 'atoms want a full outer shell' (the octet rule used as a cause), and ion formation is first taught through metals losing electrons. Chemistry-education research on this 'octet framework' (Taber) reports students judging ions such as Na⁷⁻ to be stable simply because they have a full outer shell. A full outer shell is a pattern in the ions that form, not a force that makes them form. Metal atoms, with few outer electrons that are relatively easily removed, form cations; non-metal atoms, with nearly complete outer s and p sublevels, gain the few electrons needed and form anions. So sulfur forms S²⁻, not S⁶⁺.
items.specStatementText: When metal atoms lose electrons, they form positive ions called cations. When non-metal atoms gain electrons, they form negative ions called anions.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When an iron atom, [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s², forms an ion, which electrons are removed first?
items.correct: The 4s electrons. Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶ and Fe³⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵.
items.misconception: Electrons are removed in the reverse of the filling order, so the 3d electrons are lost before the 4s electrons (Fe²⁺ would be [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s²).
items.why: The Aufbau order fills 4s before 3d, and students apply 'last in, first out' to ionization. Removing 3d electrons first is one of the most frequently reported errors in writing configurations of transition-element ions. The filling order is not the removal order. When a first-row transition element forms an ion, the 4s electrons are removed first, then 3d electrons. Iron: Fe²⁺ [Ar] 3d⁶, Fe³⁺ [Ar] 3d⁵. Copper: Cu⁺ [Ar] 3d¹⁰, Cu²⁺ [Ar] 3d⁹.
items.specStatementText: When metal atoms lose electrons, they form positive ions called cations. When non-metal atoms gain electrons, they form negative ions called anions.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When an atom forms an ion, does the number of protons change?
items.correct: No. Only the number of electrons changes. Changing the number of protons would change the element.
items.misconception: Ions form when atoms gain or lose protons, so a positive ion has extra protons and a negative ion has lost protons, while the electrons stay the same.
items.why: Protons are the positive particles, so students reason that a change in positive charge must come from a change in protons. Confusion about whether ion formation changes protons or electrons is widely reported in research on students' ideas about atomic structure. The nucleus is unchanged when an ion forms; the atomic number, and so the identity of the element, stays the same. An ion's charge comes from the difference between its fixed number of protons and its changed number of electrons, so an ion has a different electron configuration from its atom.
items.specStatementText: When metal atoms lose electrons, they form positive ions called cations. When non-metal atoms gain electrons, they form negative ions called anions.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a Na⁺ ion form only one ionic bond, because a sodium atom has only one electron to give?
items.correct: No. The number of ionic bonds an ion forms is set by how many oppositely charged ions surround it in the lattice (six for Na⁺ in NaCl), not by the number of electrons its atom lost.
items.misconception: An ion can form as many ionic bonds as the number of electrons its atom transferred: Na⁺ forms one bond, Mg²⁺ forms two.
items.why: This is the 'valency conjecture' described in Taber's research on the molecular framework for ionic bonding: students carry over the idea from covalent bonding that an atom forms a fixed number of bonds set by its electrons. Ionic bonds are not electron-pair bonds, so there is no fixed number per ion. Each ion is attracted to every oppositely charged ion around it; in sodium chloride each Na⁺ ion has six Cl⁻ neighbours and each Cl⁻ ion has six Na⁺ neighbours.
items.specStatementText: The ionic bond is formed by electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In an ionic bond, are electrons shared between the two particles?
items.correct: No. In an ionic compound the electrons have been transferred, and the ions are held by electrostatic attraction between opposite charges. Shared electron pairs are covalent bonds.
items.misconception: An ionic bond is a pair of electrons shared unequally between a metal atom and a non-metal atom.
items.why: Students meet both ionic and covalent bonding through dot-and-cross diagrams and through the idea of electronegativity difference, and they merge the two models into one 'shared but unequal' picture. Confusion between ionic and covalent bonding is widely reported. Keep the models separate at IB level: covalent bonds are shared electron pairs; ionic bonds are electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions in a lattice. The two ions in NaCl share no electrons.
items.specStatementText: The ionic bond is formed by electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is a formula containing two hydroxide ions written: Mg(OH)₂ or MgO₂H₂?
items.correct: Mg(OH)₂. A polyatomic ion is a unit; brackets show that two whole OH⁻ ions are present.
items.misconception: A polyatomic ion can be split into its atoms and the numbers multiplied out (MgO₂H₂), because the formula only needs to show how many atoms of each element are present.
items.why: Students learn to write molecular formulas by counting atoms, and they do not see the polyatomic ion as a single charged unit. Omitting brackets or multiplying out polyatomic ions is a frequent error in writing ionic formulas. The formula of an ionic compound shows its ions. Write each polyatomic ion intact, and put it in brackets when more than one is needed: Mg(OH)₂, Ca(NO₃)₂, (NH₄)₂SO₄.
items.specStatementText: The ionic bond is formed by electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is Fe₂O₃ named 'iron(III) oxygen'?
items.correct: No. The anion O²⁻ is called oxide; the name of a monatomic anion takes the suffix "-ide": oxide, chloride, nitride, sulfide.
items.misconception: The anion in a binary ionic compound is named with the name of the element, such as oxygen or chlorine.
items.why: Students name compounds by listing the elements they contain, as in the description 'a compound of iron and oxygen'. Failing to use the -ide ending is a common naming error. Binary ionic compounds are named with the cation first and the anion second, and the anion's name ends in -ide: sodium chloride, magnesium oxide, calcium nitride, iron(III) oxide.
items.specStatementText: The ionic bond is formed by electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does an oxygen atom, with six outer electrons, form O⁶⁻?
items.correct: No. Oxygen gains two electrons to complete its 2p sublevel, forming O²⁻, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶.
items.misconception: The magnitude of the charge on any ion equals the number of outer electrons of its atom, so a non-metal ion's charge is minus its number of outer electrons (O⁶⁻, Cl⁷⁻).
items.why: For metals in groups 1, 2 and 13 the charge does equal the number of outer electrons, and students carry this counting rule over to non-metals, keeping only the negative sign they know non-metal ions have. For a non-metal the charge is the number of electrons gained: −(8 − number of outer electrons). Oxygen (six outer electrons) forms O²⁻, chlorine (seven) forms Cl⁻, nitrogen (five) forms N³⁻.
items.specStatementText: The ionic bond is formed by electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does solid sodium chloride conduct electricity, given that it is made of charged ions?
items.correct: No. A current needs charged particles that can move. In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice, so the solid does not conduct.
items.misconception: A substance that contains charged particles conducts electricity, so solid ionic compounds conduct.
items.why: Students learn that a current is a flow of charge and that ionic compounds contain charged ions, and they link the two without the condition that the charges must be free to move. Conduction needs mobile charge carriers. Solid NaCl contains ions but they cannot move through the lattice; when it melts or dissolves, the ions become mobile and it conducts.
items.specStatementText: Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattice structures, represented by empirical formulas.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are the ions in sodium chloride formed when it melts or dissolves?
items.correct: No. The ions are already present in the solid lattice. Melting or dissolving only lets them move apart.
items.misconception: Solid sodium chloride consists of neutral particles (atoms or NaCl units); ions form only when it melts or dissolves in water.
items.why: Ions are first met in solutions and in electrolysis, and a solid crystal does not look as if it contains charges, so students assume the ions are produced by melting or dissolving. This is widely reported in research on students' ideas about dissolving salts. Solid NaCl is already a lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. It does not conduct because these ions cannot move, not because they are absent. Melting and dissolving separate existing ions; they do not create them.
items.specStatementText: Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattice structures, represented by empirical formulas.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do ionic solids dissolve because the solute particles fit into spaces between the solvent molecules?
items.correct: No. Whether an ionic compound dissolves depends on the attractions between the ions and the solvent molecules, not on the size of gaps between them.
items.misconception: Dissolving happens when solute particles fit into the gaps between solvent particles, so a solid dissolves in a solvent whose particles leave the right-sized spaces.
items.why: The particle model of dissolving is often illustrated by mixing peas and sand or by the volume change when alcohol and water are mixed, so students picture dissolving as filling gaps. This idea is reported in research on students' particle models of dissolving. Ions leave the lattice when solvent molecules are attracted to them strongly enough to separate them. Polar water molecules are attracted to the ions; non-polar hexane molecules are not, so NaCl dissolves in water but not in hexane.
items.specStatementText: Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattice structures, represented by empirical formulas.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the lattice enthalpy of an ionic compound set by the difference in electronegativity between its elements?
items.correct: No. At IB level lattice enthalpy is explained by the charges and radii of the ions. CsF has a larger electronegativity difference than NaF, but its larger Cs⁺ ion gives it a smaller lattice enthalpy.
items.misconception: The greater the electronegativity difference, the more ionic the compound, so the stronger its ionic bonding and the larger its lattice enthalpy.
items.why: Electronegativity difference is used to place bonds on a scale from covalent to ionic, and students take 'more ionic' to mean 'stronger ionic bond'. Electronegativity difference indicates how ionic a bond is, not how strong the attraction between the ions is. Compare lattice enthalpies using the charges of the ions (larger charge, stronger attraction) and their radii (smaller ions, stronger attraction).
items.specStatementText: Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattice structures, represented by empirical formulas.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does lattice enthalpy depend only on the charges of the ions?
items.correct: No. Ion radius matters too. NaF, NaCl and KCl all contain 1+ and 1− ions, but their lattice enthalpies decrease in that order as the ions get larger.
items.misconception: Lattice enthalpy depends only on the charges of the ions, so compounds whose ions have the same charges have the same lattice enthalpy.
items.why: The dramatic effect of charge (MgO compared with NaCl) is usually the first example students meet, and they stop there, treating charge as the only factor. Both factors matter: lattice enthalpy increases with the charges on the ions and decreases as the ions get larger. Where the charges are the same, compare the radii.
items.specStatementText: Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattice structures, represented by empirical formulas.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a compound have the properties of the elements it is made from?
items.correct: No. A compound has its own properties, which depend on its bonding and structure. Sodium is a soft, reactive metal and chlorine is a toxic green gas, but sodium chloride is a stable white crystalline solid.
items.misconception: A compound shows the properties of its elements, so sodium chloride has a high boiling point because sodium is a metal.
items.why: Students often explain properties of substances by attributing them to the individual atoms or elements present, a pattern widely reported in research on students' particle ideas. Explain the properties of an ionic compound from its structure: a lattice of oppositely charged ions held by strong electrostatic attractions, which gives low volatility and high melting points.
items.specStatementText: Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattice structures, represented by empirical formulas.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does magnesium chloride, MgCl₂, contain chlorine molecules, Cl₂?
items.correct: No. It contains Cl⁻ ions; the subscript 2 means there are two chloride ions for every Mg²⁺ ion.
items.misconception: A subscript 2 on a non-metal in an ionic formula shows a diatomic molecule of that element, so MgCl₂ contains Cl₂ molecules joined to magnesium.
items.why: Students first meet Cl₂, O₂ and H₂ as diatomic molecules and read the same symbol inside an ionic formula as the same particle. This misreading of subscripts is widely reported. In an ionic formula each subscript counts ions: MgCl₂ is one Mg²⁺ ion to two separate Cl⁻ ions, each of which is surrounded by Mg²⁺ ions in the lattice.
items.specStatementText: Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattice structures, represented by empirical formulas.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
